pitch_detail.notes: Cracks and a clean arete on the rib bounding the gully to the right of the standard one, ending on a big ledge. Shift the belay about 15 m across the ledge to the foot of the next wall.
Follow a large corner, then step onto the featured right wall to dodge the vegetation. Horizontal cracks take gear well. Belay on the ledge above.
Cut back left, pull a short bulge and gain the hanging slab left of the corner. Climb it to the arete, then go right and up a short overhanging stemming corner to a belay on a blocky arete.
Not a roped lead: move the belay along the low-angle arete to the base of the steep white wall.

Gear is sparse at first: head left up the arete on solid holds with only small wires behind flakes, about 10 m, until a stem left into the corner system is possible. Follow it to the ledge under the second white wall, then take the vertical corner on the right (awkward start, good stemming after) to the belay.
Move right into a big corner and ramp and follow it to its end. A full rope length of easy ground.

Climb the wall left of the arete using flakes and blocks, finishing right of a fresh rockfall scar. The line is not obvious, but gear is good. About 250 m of scrambling follows to the summit, on either the ridge crest or the gully to the right.

review.changed: Seven pitches written with stated grades and lengths. P6 text says 5.1 (kept literally; likely 5.1 low-angle). No crux flag: the intro puts the 5.9 crux on the fourth pitch while the list puts 5.9 on P5. No rappel table: text has no rappel stations.
review.other_findings: Intro says the 5.9 crux is on pitch 4 but the pitch list has P4 as class 3 and the 5.9 on P5. Total of listed lengths is about 295 m of roped climbing versus stored 366 m (scramble adds more).

pitch_detail.notes: Take the left arete beside the big snow-filled gully, using several bolts on the face, then cross left under a roof on flakes and blocks with crack gear. Ends at a ledge anchor. Bouldery, with a few awkward moves.

Climb the face just right of the left skyline arete past two bolts, then onto vegetated ledges. Stay right of a slung tree at about 30 m and finish with another 30 m of easy scrambling on ledges to the anchor.

Cross the final dirty ledges rightward toward a corner facing left that gives onto a splitter. Stem between the pillar to the left and the corner to the right to enter the crack. This is where the route turns classy.

Begin in the crack on the right, which thins to fingers, then shift into a pair of finger cracks to the left. Stem and grab between them; the hardest moves come near the top. Build the belay on a ledge.

Step left from the belay onto splitter fingers that widen to hands. The first few moves off the fingers are the hardest, then it eases. At roughly 25 m do not follow the straight-up splitter; instead traverse right under the roof on dike rails (about 5.8, airy, almost no gear) to an anchor below the roof.

Move right, pull the roof (about 5.10a) and enter a perfect hand-width splitter that eases to 5.8-5.9. Bring several #3 cams; it can feel run-out and you may need to walk pieces. Ends on a ledge with a two-bolt anchor. It can link with the next pitch as a full-rope stretch.
Finger crack above the ledge. The hard part is near the end where the crack flares.

A thin crack trending right across a steep slab. Stances are insecure and the crack flares, so gear is fiddly; offset nuts help and micro cams sometimes fit. Mostly slab moves using the seam and pinches, tenuous and mentally taxing. Keep going beyond the first ledges and trees to belay at a slung tree higher up. A possibly easier bypass may lie in vegetated cracks to the right.

review.changed: Eight steep-headwall pitches written. The five easier pitches above are not described in the text, so none written. Anchors recorded only where stated (P1, P2, P6; text says every pitch but P4 got bolted anchors, but the author hedges). Crux flagged where text says crux (P4, P5, P7). No rappel table: text only says most parties rap from the top of P8 with two 60 m ropes.
review.other_findings: Text says five easier pitches follow the eight described, so the real total is about 13; stored pitches is 8.

pitch_detail.notes: Hand and fist cracks and a flake. Easily linked into the next pitch.
A corner crack rising rightward into a layback past a bolt. Possibly closer to 5.9.
Slabby face trending up and right past bolts; links easily with the next pitch. A harder alternative goes up and left on face and crack at 5.10a, also about 15 m.
Easy bolted slab face.
Face climbing past a handful of bolts; links well with the next pitch.
More engaging bolted slab face climbing.
Further slabby face climbing, similar in character to the pitches below.
A rising traverse right to pull a small roof on good holds, then up into a stem box where the moves get hard.
Bolts protect a flaring crack that also takes good gear deep inside. Possibly 5.8. Links easily with the final pitch.
Easy ground to finish; then walk to the summit by the simplest line.

review.changed: Ten pitches with stated grades and lengths. The pitch-3 variant folded into P3 notes. No per-pitch bolt counts stated. No rappel table: text says the route can be rapped with a single 60 m rope but does not list stations.
review.other_findings: Listed lengths total about 200 m, matches stored 198 m.

pitch_detail.notes: Fine hand-crack climbing up a corner that faces right.
Poor-quality climbing over broken flakes and a heather gully. Trend up about 30 m to grass and heather patches, then traverse left to good ledges and stop at the foot of a very short chimney.
Climb the short chimney, move left and up a short slab, then enter a stem box, which needs a wide stem for shorter climbers. Exit right at the first chance onto a clear belay ledge.
Fun, thin fingers in a corner facing right. When the crack ends near the top, a few tricky face moves reach easier ground; go up and left to the base of the next pitch.

The standout pitch. It opens with tight hands (size 1), improves to good hands (size 2) and has a short stretch of 3s. Go left for more hands and fists, or cross to the right-hand zigzag crack from fingers to hands at several spots. A double rack makes it a committing lead.
Scramble up and right toward the summit offwidth. Without a #6 cam, the offwidth (about 5.8, two body lengths) is unprotected. Finish on the summit.

review.changed: Six pitches written; P6 has no stated grade so none given. Anchors recorded as gear because the text says all anchors are gear. No rappel info.
review.other_findings: Stored pitches is 6, consistent. Listed lengths total about 180 m versus stored 213 m.

pitch_detail.notes: Start in the base of a big chimney and stem up to the top of the landing. Carrying the pack here is miserable for the second, so consider hauling or leading with it.
Good hand and fist jams lead up a short slab, then a finger to hand-size crack finishes at the landing above. Keep your mid-size cams for this one, since gear anchors eat up the larger pieces.
Reach the top of the shelf, then a dynamic move to a jug above on thin feet. Shorter climbers may find the reach hard.
Scramble through the flakes to the col between the North and South Spires.

review.changed: Four pitches, no grades or lengths because the text gives none per pitch. Anchors gear on all belays per text. No rappel info (descent is a walk-off).

pitch_detail.notes: Obvious cracks with some fixed gear, including a stuck cam that gives a fun stem. Grade is approximate. Belay on the ledge at the horizontal.
Shift right along the ledge to a short splitter of finger size. Set the belay to the left, ahead of the corner that faces left. This pitch probably combines with the first.

Step down, then take steep cracks until the corner on the right becomes reachable. Follow that to a slab and finish by a broad flake or the wide crack on its left. Belay either from a horn of boulder or by building one in the corner.
Scramble to the splitter cracks, follow them and some slabby ground to the flat part of the ridge. Grade is approximate.
Either simul-climb or untie and scramble about 100 m to the foot of the headwall cracks.
Perfect cracks up to blockier terrain above. Build an anchor there, or lower or downclimb to the flat area below. Grade is approximate.
Pick carefully up loose, stacked blocks to the summit.

review.changed: Seven pitches written; no lengths except the ~100 m pitch 5. No rappel table: text mentions a neglected rap route down the south face without stations.

pitch_detail.notes: Begin by scrambling a grubby corner to a ledge roughly 10 m up. Then follow the dirty corner system to the foot of a clean chimney; skip the grassy corner trending right.

A clean square chimney with plentiful gear in its back. After it widens to a stem, commit leftward to a steep hand crack (the crux) into a flare. The stance near the flare's base is bad, so it is easy to climb too far.
A thin step right past a fixed nut, then up the corner that faces left until the angle relents. Short chimney (about 3 m) to the left, climb it and belay on the pedestal, which is the best stance.

Original line: stay in the left corner system, go up and left over a small roof (extend gear to limit drag), then a wide crack (#4 or bigger), onto the slab with compression, to the base of a chimney. A hard thin 5.11+ variation (40 m, right-facing corner past a change into a left-facing corner) is now often climbed; it needs many micro nuts and tiny cams, and few of its original pitons remain.
Struggle up the chimney, step right to the belay ledge. If you took the 5.11+ variation, you walk left across a thin ledge into a chimney and climb it, ending 10 m above your belay.

Wide chimney first, then leave it rightward for a crack that goes from fingers to hands. The crux is a short stretch where the crack is shallow and flaring; easier angle follows. Move right and up to belay under the steep top wall, or run straight into the final pitch.

A brief, steep crack in a small corner facing right gets over the headwall; friendly horizontals make it less intimidating than it looks. Top out on the ridge; a summit block with a 5.9 offwidth lies farther north.

review.changed: Seven pitches following the original (5.11-) line; the 5.11+ P4/P5 variation folded into notes. No anchors stated. No rappel table: text mentions only one bolted rappel from the ridge.

pitch_detail.notes: Scramble from the west to the foot of a corner on the right side of the tallest tower (the summit). Short corner to a ledge, then a second corner with a #4-size crack on the right and finger or ring locks on the left. Leave to the right for a rappel station, or to the left across a loose slab to another station, which is better for belaying but harder to exit.

Starts about below the left-hand station. Mantle to a ledge, then choose between an offwidth chimney on the right, an offset crack from hands to fingers straight above the station, or hands to offwidth on the left. Stop just under the headwall of the summit block and build a gear anchor.

Skirt the headwall on the right: step onto an exposed ledge and up a short vertical fist-size crack to a flat edge (a parallel hand crack lies just right). Pull over onto low-angle slab to the summit block and mantle the summit boulder once the second arrives.

review.changed: Three pitches, no grades or lengths (none stated). Only the P2 anchor is stated as gear; left unfilled for others. No rappel table.

pitch_detail.notes: Climb a wet dike, step left onto the beautiful left-slanting finger crack and go fast on thin locks to a belay at the base of a roof.
Tackle the roof by the first crack that peels off leftward from the main line, passing a small stem-box roof to reach a stance.

A flaring crack system with a brief boulder problem across to vertical cracks on the right keeps you on the main line. When the flare dies out and gets very hard, tiptoe left on small edges and knobs about 4 m to a second crack, then return right to a big comfortable ledge.
A clean dihedral to another belay ledge.
Trend right over broken ground between the main wall and a small flake tower, passing around it out of your belayer's sight. Black lichen cracks and flakes lead toward the top.
Loose blocks reach the top of the tower. Bring a tag line for the descent, since some rappels exceed 35 m.

review.changed: Six pitches written; no lengths given. Crux flagged on P3 as top grade. Anchors: text only says bolted anchors in general, so not set per pitch. No rappel table.
review.other_findings: Text describes 6 pitches (last 4th class); stored pitches is 5.

pitch_detail.notes: From the foot of the wall, thin cracks with crisp edges (to the left of the offwidth) lead to a bolted anchor beneath the big chimney. The length shifts with how much snow lies at the base.
Ease up the chimney roughly 6 m, then cross left over crimps with two bolts to a lovely right-facing corner. It ends at a bolted anchor on a small foothold ledge.
Follow the corner about 5 m, then step right into a second one. This sustained thin corner has a distinct crux and some face moves, ending on a good ledge under the large roof.

Two bolts of face climbing reach the roof, which you traverse leftward past another bolt to a ledge, then 5.9 cracks with a brief offwidth section to the ledge and anchor used for the descent. Clip a long sling to it and walk 15 m along the ledge to the next anchor under a finger crack, and belay there.

Start up a 5.11 finger crack to the roof, then pull it steeply with two bolts for protection and stand on a stance. Two further bolts guard slab and face moves, after which a crack heads up-left to a bolted anchor. Sustained, endurance-style climbing.
A hard boulder problem opens the pitch off the belay. Two bolts follow, then a 5.11 finger crack splits the headwall and ends at a two-bolt anchor.
Gain a big ledge about 5 m up, then cross to the right until beneath a steep flake. Layback and jam the flake with five bolts for protection, finishing at an anchor on the slab.
Move right off the anchor. Loose blocks and a few body lengths of 5.4 precede third-class terrain up to the summit. The first ascent team lowered down this pitch rather than climbing it.

review.changed: Eight pitches with stated grades, lengths and bolted belays. Bolt counts only where unambiguous (none set as the field). No rappel table: text says all anchors have rap hangers and the route was rapped but lists no stations.

pitch_detail.notes: From the ledge above the approach slabs, start just up and left on a right-trending crack. Climb the groove, continue right to pass the bulge, then back left on slabs to the belay. The pitch can be skipped by taking the long leftward ramp (maybe 65 m, with brief simul-climbing).
A few steep steps, then trend up and left past two bolts, through a small bulge and back right into an easier groove to a large ledge.
An obvious ramp leading left to the belay.
Go up the right-facing corner to a big ledge, then the large left-trending crack, with one steep move to a belay ledge.

A very long pitch; a 60 m rope barely reaches, and brief simul-climbing may be needed otherwise. Climb the crack right of the belay ledge, the corner above, step left over a small overlap, and continue up grooves to a ledge.
Walk right along the ledge to the next belay.
Another rope stretcher. Up and right toward flakes, above them to a bolt, up and left to a ledge, then left along it to a belay. A long rappel from here reaches the P5 anchor.
Clip a bolt above the anchor, then take the groove if dry or the blunt arete to its left, and go up and right through broken ground to a belay below steeper rock.
Climb the corner that breaks the steep wall to a grassy ledge, continue on ledges and squeeze through cedars. Above is a small chimney flake with a bolt, then heather to a big ledge.

Climb the big groove up and right from the belay. When it gets steep and dirty, find a bolt to the left and leave the groove on steep, fun rock. Keep heading upward to a ledge with another bolt, and follow sporadic cracks to a belay below a bulge.
Up left to the weak line through the bulge. Small slabs and ledges with a bolt about halfway lead to a belay on a little ledge.
Rope stretcher: easy climbing with little protection at first, steeper at the end.
Up and left around the wall above the belay, then walk through bushes left to low-angle heather ledges. A spacious ledge down and left offers a bivy for at least three and possibly water.
Nice slabby rock, then heather ledges, a short wall, and a tunnel up through cedar to a belay ledge below steepening rock.
Bolt above the anchor, another above, then step out right to a third. Head left to a heather ledge, right along it to two more bolts up a steep corner, then up and right around a bulge to the anchor.
Up and left in a large open corner, then back up and right in an obvious corner system to a belay on an exposed pinnacle.
An awkward leaning corner to the anchor under the very steep flakes.
Heave on the flake over the anchor (or pull on bolts) through the first steep section; it then eases, and a few bolts protect the last moves into a belay inside a large chimney.
Clip a bolt and step out right into very exposed position, climb a ramp on great holds, step over a dwarf tree, and continue along a ledge to a weakness on the left. Belay above a short step.

Go around the wall above the anchor to the right; the face looking into the big gully has a fine crack system that angles up to the ridge crest. Cross the crest and follow the thin fin to a large horn where it rejoins the mountain. Rope drag is a problem.

Descend into the gully and cross it, then climb the large corner (right-facing) to a ledge. Work back right until a bolt appears to the left, clip it and another farther left, and gain the ledge above. Take the groove at the ledge's left edge to another ledge, go up and right on easier ground, then back left to the ridge crest and belay just around it.

Go left along the large ledge, find gear and climb toward the chimney visible above; horns above it can be slung for the belay. The summit is an easy walk up and right. The route finishes just beneath the summit tower, and in dry conditions the descent needs no snow travel.

review.changed: All 22 pitches with stated grades and lengths; crux set on the two 5.10 pitches (top grade). Bolt counts omitted for ambiguity. No rappel table (only a note on a long rappel from the top of P7).
review.other_findings: Route grade 5.10- R vs 5.10 pitches in text; otherwise consistent.

pitch_detail.notes: Start off the snow on the left side of the scoop in the rock scar. Hand cracks lead to a possible gear belay across the scoop. Length depends on snow depth.
Cross the scoop and continue up the thinner slabby corner to a two-bolt anchor. P1 and P2 can be done as one pitch with a 70 m rope.
Climb the corner above and pull a small overhang, step left into a shallow left-facing corner, then an easy ramp to flakes going back right. Hand-traverse them to the belay.
A long pitch with three separate hard sections: thin tips at the bottom, a stem corner, then left past a bolt onto the arete and back right into the corner for thin stemming moves with small gear.

A steep fist crack off the belay, then layback the bulge with its wide pod (a #5 helps). Above, clip a bolt and move up-left into a right-leaning corner with a hand crack, then easier ground to a large ledge, traversed up-left to an anchor with rings under a groove that trends right.
Enter the groove, clip two knifeblade pitons, then face climb to a two-bolt anchor.
A finger crack, traversing left then back right to the main line. Place gear at the roof and pull it; mostly 5.10 fingers aside from the roof. Anchor is left on the slab above.

Clip a bolt, traverse the slab right to a left-leaning, left-facing corner. Climb it with micro cams and small wires past two pins, then into the main corner (a pin and two bolts, then gear) to a bolted belay.

Head for the base of a steeper left-facing wall split by several good-looking cracks. Mostly easy climbing apart from a brief finger-crack crux. Ascend the corner until just under a grassy ledge, move right and cross ledgy ground to the anchor, which makes a decent bivy ledge.
The best of the cracks. The belay is on the left but it links easily with the next.
Right-hand crack on good hands, thinning to a delicate finish into an alcove with a bolted belay.

Climb the left crack about 5 m, then make reachy face moves across to the crack running alongside the arete, and follow it past the lip to a bolted belay. May feel harder than the grade and could use scrubbing.
An easy but run-out chimney to the pinnacle top; links with P12 on a 70 m rope.
Bouldery moves up a thin left-slanting crack past three bolts, easing to a good belay ledge.
Follow a fist crack up the pillar's left flank, then a thin splitter hand crack through the headwall above; rest first. Doubles from #0.5 to #1 suffice, though extras of #0.75 or #1 are useful.
The crack opens up as the slope eases back. Pass the bulge on its right side and carry on up a groove to a bolted belay. The summit may be a fourth-class scramble above.

review.changed: All 16 pitches. P1 and P2 kept separate (text grades them separately). P2 anchor is stated; P1 only a possible gear belay. Crux only on top-grade pitch P14. No rappel table: text gives only a partial rap sequence for the lower pitches.

pitch_detail.notes: Start with a flake facing left, which gives onto a ledge; a dark slot then leads to a little roof. Belay to its right. Quoted length is 20 to 30 m.
Go left from the belay and up a face crack that leans left to a ledge. Can be aided at 5.11 C1.
The crack continues, widening. Go by an old piton anchor and finish leftward past a bolt, to a belay below a splitter in a left-facing corner.
Follow the splitter corner crack, which varies between hand and finger widths, to a belay off to the left near the summit of a pillar.
Tips-size crack giving way to face moves, with two bolts, reaching an anchored stance. Gear is nuts and small micro cams.
Small edges to bouldery roof moves, with eight bolts. Can be aided at 5.11b A0.
Hand crack to an overhang, then left up hand and finger cracks beside an arete. Rappel this one as a 30 m drop, since the rope may jam in the crack.
Up an open book corner with a tips-size crux, then into a corner on the right, reaching the belay. Be ready to simul-climb; a rope stretcher on the way down. A two-pitch 5.10+ variation exists.

Go left from the belay up a golden corner facing left, then again left into a shallow corner with a crack and a fixed lost arrow. A few feet above, move left into a further corner and belay. The descent from here is a rappel to the midpoint anchor of P8.
About 30 m of run-out laybacking (around 5.9) on a corner and flake, then rightward across face holds to a corner facing left that leads to a belay ledge.
A fingery corner that faces right, up to a ledge; easy moves right, then a face crack to a second right-facing corner. Climb it to a ramp that leads left to the belay.
Left to an overhanging corner and slot, then a wide corner crack, and traverse right 10 m to a large, semi-hanging boulder belay.
Climb a chimney directly, or go right over broken ground and back left, to a belay in fourth class.
Scramble to the north summit.

review.changed: All 14 pitches with stated grades and lengths. No crux flags. No rappel table: only three scattered rappel remarks (P9, P8, P7), not a station list.

pitch_detail.notes: A steep right-facing dihedral holds two cracks; a slight overhang is passed on its left. An obvious crack continues beyond the first anchor, widening into an offwidth as the wall steepens, and solid 5.10 offwidth leads onto lower-angle rock and another anchor. One climber rated it near 5.10c.

Keep following the crack about 3 m to a second one angling up-right. Traverse it by hand until it turns vertical, pass an anchor and enter a perfect 2 inch crack. Layback right from a wide crack to reach a dihedral and its anchor. One party came up roughly 1.5 m short and simul-climbed to reach it.
Continue the dihedral to an overhang, power through a crack near its left side, then traverse back right to a crack that goes up to a belay about 6 m below the crux roof. Probably hard 5.10.

The crux of the climb. Climb about 6 m to beneath a large corner roof, place a couple of pieces at the lip and go through it without lingering. Past an anchor and over another bulge, overhanging, to a good belay stance. Not thought to be too hard.
Follow cracks up and a little right in a dihedral facing left; the crack curls back left along a big flake to a stance beneath a splitter of wide hands to fists.

The finale: a steep crack of hand and fist size runs for around 100 ft before dividing. Left is about 5.8 and easier, but right is the better line, a hand traverse in a very exposed position into a perfect crack that angles up and back left. Place a final piece where it ends and finish with some hard face moves. Long, though a 60 m rope still reaches.

review.changed: Six long pitches written as described (no grades per pitch because the author only gives impressions). Anchors not stated per pitch. No rappel table: text says rap the route with two ropes.
review.other_findings: Text describes 6 long pitches (about 275 m total) while stored pitches is 11; likely the 11 comes from shorter splits using the existing anchors.

pitch_detail.notes: A corner to a gear belay where the crack splits. The last rappel station is visible across to the right under a small roof.
A layback with good feet and plenty of gear, belaying on gear atop the corner where it eases. Cleaned in 2010.
Up about 8 m, right past one 5.8 move, to a bolted belay (a rappel station) about 5 m left of the corner.
Up a broken gully past another rap station to a steeper block that looks like a layback; belay beneath it on gear.
Pass the layback block and run up a stem box in a long, enjoyable pitch to belay from slings on a horn at the foot of the huge white wall.

Take the finger ledge rightward and a bit upward in a superb position; clip the rap station and an ancient bolt as protection. Then go right up the arete and crack, returning left to another rap station for the belay.

Traverse down 10 m left, then go up the right-facing corner by laybacking, stemming and body-jamming, exiting up-left or up-right to fixed belays. Burly moves but plentiful gear in all sizes; bring many long slings.

review.changed: Seven pitches with stated grades and lengths. P3/P6 anchors are rap stations per text. No rappel table: text lists no station sequence.

pitch_detail.notes: From a slab right of the ridge, cracks and flakes lead to the ridge crest and a belay.
Continue along the ridge crest to a belay.
Stay on the crest until it steepens, then cracks and grooves left of the crest to a ledge belay.
A finger and hand crack just right of the crest goes through a small bulge; continue to a small ledge belay.
Cracks on the left of the ridge reach easy ground; a flake and then a chimney, again left of the crest, end at a sloping ledge.
Traverse right on a handrail to a big left-facing dihedral and climb it to an alcove behind a jagged block.
Continue up the dihedral, then a crack to a large scree-covered ledge.
Walk up the scree ledge to its top and belay at a bivy site.
Chimney and cracks through blocks, ending below the foot of a steep wall.
Go left up a short, hard crack to a ledge, then traverse right to a pair of dihedrals and take the right-hand one to a large flat ledge.

Beginning of the upper headwall, called the Great White Headwall. A strenuous hand and fist crack in a right-facing corner at the left side of the ledge leads to another ledge. A second crack in a left-facing corner follows, until you can exit left onto a steep face and a belay ledge.
Balance right into a corner and follow it past blocks and a hard squeeze, possible with a pack, to a belay at the foot of a gully.
Ascend the gully until it narrows and steepens into a corner. Use the second crack on the left wall, belaying at the base of a corner that faces right.
The long dihedral that faces right ends at an anchor of two pins in a small notch.
The crux, and it is optional to aid it. Move out left on small holds and make one hard move around the arete, then finish up an easy gully. Tensioning the traverse at A0 is another way past.

review.changed: All 15 pitches with stated grades (none have lengths). No rappel table: descent text gives counts and generalities, not a station list.

pitch_detail.notes: A series of short vertical flakes, then slightly rambling terrain to a roomy belay ledge.
A slab with a few tricky moves to a prominent undercling, mantle into a left corner and stem or layback about 8 m, then step right onto the face on big crimps to a roomy ledge.
Up right on positive holds, left onto the face, then stem the lower dihedral, which has good feet and hands, and return to the face for the anchors.
Follow the left-trending flake right of the belay to the vertical upper dihedral, make an exposed, committing step into it and stem to the top.
Follow bolts trending right to a steep topout, a big mantle onto a slightly downsloping ledge, then around to the right to the anchors.

From a tight belay ledge climb sloping holds, then a long layback flake of about 9 m to the final roof. Step right with a committing move on small crimps and carefully round the corner to the final arete.
Traverse along the arete about 30 m to the next station; from there a steeper section with good holds. Stay near the edge; bolts are on the right.
Straight up the arete hugging the edge on solid rock, staying left of the bolts for handholds, to another bolted station, then exposed third-class ground to the summit.

review.changed: Eight pitches with stated grades and lengths; rap rings on all stations per text. No rappel table: text says four doubled rappels with two 70 m ropes but lists no stations.
review.other_findings: Listed lengths total about 255 m versus stored 305 m. Stored discipline sport; the text says fully bolted.

pitch_detail.notes: Start by traversing the big grassy ledge about 20 m right of the neighbouring route. Pull the bulge above the belay, then climb flakes toward the base of a blocky orange corner that faces left, to a bolted station.

Avoid the corner by working up and to its left, with gear in small overlaps. At a bulge pull round the corner and head right to another corner facing left; climb it to a wide sloping ledge. A gear belay is optional there, or push on mindful of rope drag. Cross right to a third corner and climb to the bolted station beneath a finger crack.

A high-quality splitter finger crack. Trace the roof up and rightward, then step left to surmount it. Go up and left, clipping a single bolt, to a station at the base of a conspicuous corner system that faces left.
Follow the corner system on the left for about 35 m with options; as the main corner turns blocky, escape right via cracks and blocks to a big comfortable ledge on the prow with a bolted station.
A couple of steps above the belay, stem out of a small alcove to the ridge crest, then scramble along it to easier ground and a gear belay.

review.changed: Five pitches with stated grades and lengths. No rappel table: text describes rapping from the top of P4 with an 80 m or two 60 m ropes and the normal descent, not a station list.

pitch_detail.notes: Start in a slab groove between two small walls, about 25 m, and clip a bolt at its top. Then 25 m of low-angle, run-out slab crosses to a flat ledge with a bolt anchor, slightly left, below a left-facing corner.

Climb the corner above the belay, which has good crack gear. Near the top, place the last piece in a sickle-shaped undercling and slab diagonally left (run-out) to the anchor under the big pinnacle. Avoid the pinnacle's lower corner, which blanks out. An option at 5.6 climbs right of the anchor and traverses back left along a ledge.

The steep pinnacle wall on the left of the belay is face climbed with tricky moves; two key pieces cover the crux. It leads to a face crack that begins thin and widens to a lovely 5.6 hand crack. The bolted belay sits on a small ledge to the right.
Continue up the crack past a large shrub and ring bolts on the right halfway up, to a second shrub with a bolted anchor just below. A rope stretcher.

Top out the pinnacle via the corner facing right (5.7). From its ledge, a 15 ft slab wall is bouldered (5.9, no protection) to a small ledge with ring bolts above. At 5.6 you can instead go 15 ft left to easier crack and face and return right to the bolts.

Shift up and left 15 ft to a dike with good features, then fairly solid, enjoyable face climbing leads diagonally right, past an old piton, to a bolted anchor under a steep wall. P5 and P6 link into a 60 m rope stretcher using long slings.
Head up and right to a short, steep wall where a bolt guards the 5.9 crux at the lip. Easier, crumbly face climbing continues up and rightward to a bolted anchor.

Cross 15 ft right to a fun layback flake and layback it about 30 ft, then step right onto large crumbly holds. Continue on the crack and face along its front to a brief steep crux, protected by underclings and a small nut placed at the lip. A shallow groove beyond ends at a bolted anchor on a ledge. The 2022 rockfall started here, and the original belay bolts sit about 5 m up and right over the scar. The leftward traverse offers no gear.

Now leaving the Yak Crack line. Climb 10 m up crumbly rock, left along a solid horizontal dike to many flakes, undercling left, then to the highest undercling at a roof. Move left (5.9, awkward) to the Cave corner, but it is better to go right onto the cave arete and climb about 10 m to a big ledge with a bolted belay on the right.
Walk across the ledge on top of the through-flake to a belay on bolts at the left.
Up a flake and ramp leftward, then back right somewhat. Two bolts once the good crack ends.

Face climb 3 m to a bolt, up and right to another, back left and up to a corner (bolt on the left arete), climb right of it on dishes and flakes, then a faint line up and right past more bolts to a belay on a small right-facing ramp that is not visible until 5 m below. About five bolts. Poor route-finding can lead into 5.10a.

Up the flake above the belay, directly where it goes right, or left up good face cracks, to a ledge, then a low-angle slab with three bolts, cleaned of lichen. Belay at a bolted stance on the ledge above. This is where you would rappel from; walking off is faster.

Run-out slab with no protection to trees. The easiest escape is a hard-left traverse of 10 m to the lowest trees, then the dirt gully up. Then hike and scramble to the top, passing the subsummit on the right.
